prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Traffic facility poles: When traffic management facilities such as traffic signal lights, traffic monitoring poles, and traffic sign boards are arranged in the median/side median, they shall be aligned with the centerline of streetlights and other facilities within the median. Where there is no side median or central median, traffic signal lights, traffic monitoring poles, and traffic sign boards shall be arranged within the sidewalk facility zone and shall not occupy or obstruct sidewalk passage or the area adjacent to pedestrian crosswalk lines. Traffic facility poles should, as far as possible, achieve “one pole for multiple uses.” When streetlight poles and sign poles are combined into one pole, full consideration shall be given to the issue of traffic signs being obscured by the light below (“lamp-shadow blindness”), and the relationship among various poles and roadside trees shall be coordinated comprehensively to avoid roadside trees obstructing signs, monitoring devices, and traffic signal lights. 2. Central median guardrails and side median guardrails: Their layout should start from the stop line at intersections and shall not hinder normal vehicle movement. Pedestrian guardrails that are not fully isolating or serve a warning function may adopt a post-and-chain form. 4.  Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups

- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)

- Accessibility
Safety

Comfort

- Psychological Comfort

Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

For systems that are severely damaged or can no longer operate normally, reconstruction shall be carried out according to actual needs. 4.3 Urban Furniture 4.3.1 Traffic Management Facilities The color, form, style, and other aspects of traffic management facilities in the same city should be as unified as possible; roads in certain special areas may be designed with appropriate distinctive features. 1. Traffic facility poles: When traffic management facilities such as traffic signal lights, traffic monitoring poles, and traffic sign boards are arranged in the median/side median, they shall be aligned with the centerline of streetlights and other facilities within the median. Where there is no side median or central median, traffic signal lights, traffic monitoring poles, and traffic sign boards shall be arranged within the sidewalk facility zone and shall not occupy or obstruct sidewalk passage or the area adjacent to pedestrian crosswalk lines. Traffic facility poles should, as far as possible, achieve “one pole for multiple uses.” When streetlight poles and sign poles are combined into one pole, full consideration shall be given to the issue of traffic signs being obscured by the light below (“lamp-shadow blindness”), and the relationship among various poles and roadside trees shall be coordinated comprehensively to avoid roadside trees obstructing signs, monitoring devices, and traffic signal lights. 2. Central median guardrails and side median guardrails: Their layout should start from the stop line at intersections and shall not hinder normal vehicle movement. End warning signs shall be set at the starting point, and reflectors, reflective film, etc. shall be installed on the posts. The length and height of each guardrail panel shall take into account functional requirements, manufacturing process, and the requirements of the deployment area. Figure 4.3-1 Example of Central Median Guardrail 3. Pedestrian guardrails shall start from the end position of the sidewalk curb ramp and be laid close to the inner edge line of the curb. For guardrails at locations with fall hazards, the clear spacing of vertical members shall not be greater than 0.11 m, and structures with footholds are not recommended. Pedestrian guardrails that are not fully isolating or serve a warning function may adopt a post-and-chain form. 4. Vehicle-stopping bollards / vehicle-blocking stones: Materials shall be selected according to the location and functional requirements, using durable materials such as stone, cast iron, stainless steel, galvanized steel, or aluminum alloy. The spacing between bollards should be 1.3 m–1.5 m, and the height should be 0.4 m–0.6 m. Reflective film, warning lights, etc. shall be installed. 151 Figure 4.3-2 Example of Vehicle-Stopping Bollards / Vehicle-Blocking Stones 5. Purpose of Formulation Under the macro guidance of the “General Provisions,” these Detailed Rules aim at the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads, and are expanded and implemented from four directions: human-oriented, quality-oriented, distinctive, and intelligent. They interpret the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads in the form of colorful labels, and create urban colorful roads unique to Suzhou. ➢ Human-oriented: Starting from the users of Suzhou’s urban roads, and taking the public’s experience of urban road space as the benchmark, fully consider the comfort, safety, and convenience of public activities, and realize the value shift from “vehicle-centered” to “people-centered.” ➢ Quality-oriented: Vigorously improve the travel quality of people and vehicle traffic in Suzhou, and emphasize the public space function of roads. Appropriately raise the standards for urban road design, construction, and maintenance, extend road service life, and improve users’ comfort of experience. Reflect a road construction level of high appearance and high standards, with attention to detail and control. ➢ Distinctive: Adapt measures to local conditions, and through the embedding of Suzhou-style elements and the creation of road characteristic scenes, highlight Suzhou’s distinctive urban character of integration between tradition and modernity, so that urban roads become an important carrier and display space for the “Jiangnan culture” brand, and continue the city’s historical and cultural lineage. ➢ Intelligent: Deploy intelligent sensing devices along the roadside, together with cloud service platforms, computing and communication facilities, and through data technologies such as autonomous driving and vehicle-road coordination, realize a travel experience of deep interaction among people, vehicles, and road space, assist safe driving and autonomous driving, and create demonstration roads with Suzhou’s smart-city characteristics. 2. Consider the daily use needs of residents and facilitate everyday social interaction. • Create a personalized spatial environment. Spatial requirements: • Use road space efficiently and ensure sufficient slow-mobility space with shaded pedestrian areas. • Roads of this type should be designed with smaller turning radii. • Where conditions permit, motor-vehicle lanes may be compressed and a single-sided public-service/facility zone set up. • Actively create building setbacks, encourage buildings and sidewalks to be connected, maintain the same setback interface, and reduce the large variation between road-space and building-space. Facility requirements: • Provide convenient and safe pedestrian crossings; for life-service roads of higher grade, encourage elevated pedestrian crossings, curb extensions, and other traffic-calming facilities, and speed limits. • Encourage the use of green forms such as lawns, sparse tree stands, rows of trees, shrubs, and planting of trees and other vegetation to create a people-oriented, green environment. • Consider larger-canopy trees; for tall planting, the root space should be relatively small to ensure pedestrian passage space. • Use non-open interfaces on both sides as the main form; road greenery may be used to create transparent, screened, separated, and other visual-control effects. 9 Landscape-recreation roads Recommendations for upgrading and improving interface types General requirements: • Encourage the integration of urban landscape and recreational functions, balancing landscape and leisure activities with residents’ daily travel needs. • Increase the amount of green space along the line to avoid vegetation becoming an obstacle to activities.
